The little auk (Alle alle) is a high-Arctic seabird that exhibits a tightly constrained breeding schedule due to the short polar summer. During the incubation period, the female typically lays a single egg that weighs approximately 31.6 grams [Ww0 = approximately 31.6 grams]. This investment represents a substantial fraction of the adult female's body mass, a common pattern among alcids. The egg is incubated in deep crevices within talus slopes where the attending parents regulate the thermal environment; field measurements indicate that the egg is maintained at a temperature of around 36 °C [T = 36 °C] during the incubation period, which lasts 29 days [ab = 29 days]. This relatively short developmental period is necessary to ensure that the chick hatches with sufficient time to grow and fledge before the onset of winter. The synchronised hatching of colonies across the Thulean region suggests that photoperiod and temperature cues strongly govern this critical life-history schedule.

Once the egg hatches, the nestling emerges at a remarkably low body mass compared to the adult. Newly hatched chicks weigh just 21.5 grams [Wwb = 21.5 grams], a value that places them among the lighter hatchlings for an alcid of this size. This low birth mass necessitates an intense period of parental provisioning, with both adults making numerous foraging trips to nearby polynyas to collect crustaceans and small fish. The ability of the chick to survive this early stage depends heavily on the quality and quantity of food delivered by the parents. Under the standard thermal conditions of the nest microclimate, which is maintained close to the adult core body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], the chick undergoes rapid somatic growth. The nestling phase is remarkably brief, and the young bird reaches the fledging stage at just 27.5 days after hatching [tx = 27.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C].

During this post-hatching development, the chick must accumulate sufficient energy reserves to sustain itself after it leaves the colony. The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown adult little auk is 163.5 grams [Wwi = 163.5 grams], a mass that is typically achieved by the end of the first summer. The rapid growth from the 21.5 gram neonate to this adult mass is fuelled by a high metabolic rate and constant foraging effort by the parents. This growth trajectory is one of the fastest among the Alcini, a necessity driven by the extreme time constraints of the high-Arctic breeding season. In contrast to the low incubation temperature, the active chick and adult maintain a body temperature near 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C] during peak metabolic activity. This elevated thermal setpoint is critical for maintaining the enzymatic efficiency needed to process the large quantities of lipid-rich prey required for such accelerated weight gain.

The maximum lifespan for this species, based on comparative data from the closely related Cassin's auklet, is estimated at 16.2 years [am = 16.2 years] when measured at a standard active body temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C].
